title: Realtime Delivery Event Retention Rules for Recovering Missed Map Updates
author: DemetriusReed2163
summary: Short answer: keep a short, durable event window for the delivery tracking map, make reconnects request a cursor, and treat a snapshot plus replay as the recovery contract. Live delivery is a performance path; retention is what makes it correct after a phone sleeps, a tunnel drops, or a browser process restarts. I build RAG and agent features in Python, so I tend to test the boring boundary first: what happens when the client comes back with an old cursor? A map that looks realtime during a clean demo can still show a courier ten minutes behind if its retention policy only serves the happy path. The useful design is a small event log, explicit expiry semantics, and an eval harness that measures recovery rather than just median latency. Start with the recovery contract The delivery service should publish immutable location events with a monotonic sequence per delivery (or per map shard). An event might contain delivery_id , sequence , observed_at , a coarse location, and a state such as en_route or delivered . The map gateway keeps the newest sequence it has rendered. On reconnect, the client sends that cursor; the gateway either replays the missing range or returns a fresh snapshot followed by newer events. That distinction matters. A websocket is a transport, not a history database. WebRTC data channels can carry low-latency application data, but the W3C recommendation leaves application-level ordering, persistence, and replay policy to the system around the channel. In other words, reconnect behavior is your protocol to define. The retention clock should start when an event is accepted by the log, not when a viewer happens to receive it. Keep a separate observed_at (device time) and ingested_at (server time); mobile clocks drift, and using device time for expiry can silently delete recent updates. A compact index keyed by (delivery_id, sequence) makes a range query predictable even when many customers watch the same city. How should realtime event retention and delivery backfill work? Here is a deliberately plain Python gateway sketch. It uses an abstract store so the policy can be tested without choosing a broker or database. The important behavior is the response shape: replay when the cursor is inside the retained window, snapshot when it is too old, and noop when the client is current. from dataclasses import dataclass from datetime import datetime , timedelta , timezone from typing import Protocol @dataclass ( frozen = True ) class LocationEvent : delivery_id : str sequence : int lat : float lon : float state : str ingested_at : datetime class EventStore ( Protocol ): def newest_sequence ( self , delivery_id : str ) -> int : ... def oldest_sequence ( self , delivery_id : str ) -> int : ... def after ( self , delivery_id : str , sequence : int ) -> list [ LocationEvent ]: ... def snapshot ( self , delivery_id : str ) -> dict : ... def recover ( store : EventStore , delivery_id : str , cursor : int | None ) -> dict : newest = store . newest_sequence ( delivery_id ) oldest = store . oldest_sequence ( delivery_id ) if cursor is None or cursor < oldest - 1 : return { " kind " : " snapshot " , " state " : store . snapshot ( delivery_id ), " cursor " : newest , } if cursor >= newest : return { " kind " : " noop " , " cursor " : newest } return { " kind " : " replay " , " events " : [ event . __dict__ for event in store . after ( delivery_id , cursor )], " cursor " : newest , } The oldest - 1 check is the part I would put under an eval before wiring a production stream. It prevents a partial replay from masquerading as a complete map. If a snapshot and replay race with a new event, the server should return the snapshot cursor and then replay strictly after that cursor. Clients apply events only when the sequence is exactly the next expected value; a gap triggers recovery again. Make the cursor boring. One early mistake is retaining by row count: “keep the last 10,000 updates.” That gives a different user experience in a quiet suburb and a stadium district. A time window, plus a maximum byte budget, is easier to explain. For example, a product might retain 15 minutes of fine-grained locations and a longer, coarser history elsewhere. The exact duration is a product and privacy decision, not a universal realtime constant. Choosing a window without lying to yourself Retention has three competing consumers: reconnects, delayed readers, and operations. Measure each separately. A reconnect SLO such as “99% of sessions recover by replay” is only meaningful when paired with a maximum offline interval and the event rate per delivery. If the event rate is 2 events per second and the worst expected offline gap is 90 seconds, a single delivery can produce 180 events before the viewer returns. Multiply that by active deliveries, serialization overhead, and fan-out when sizing the log. I keep a tiny replay evaluator beside the service. It feeds synthetic disconnects at 5, 30, and 120 seconds, then checks that the rendered state equals a reference fold of the events. It also checks duplicate delivery, out-of-order frames, and a cursor just one sequence older than the retained boundary. Your mileage may vary: real radio gaps are bursty, and a percentile from staging does not predict a lift in an underground garage. The retention policy should be visible in metrics: oldest retained sequence, replay-hit rate, snapshot-fallback rate, bytes per delivery, and time from ingest to render. Log the cursor decision, but avoid putting precise coordinates in general application logs. Sampling a hashed delivery identifier is enough to connect a failed recovery to a trace while reducing exposure. Measure it. Failure modes that look like latency Most “slow map” reports are consistency failures. A client may reconnect successfully, receive an old snapshot, and then apply a newer event from a second connection. Without a single sequence gate, the marker jumps backward. Another common case is acknowledging a message before the application persists its cursor; a process crash then causes a replay storm. Persist the cursor after applying the event, and make event application idempotent. Backfill can also overload the live path. Put a bounded limit on replay batches and yield between batches so a single mobile client cannot monopolize a shard. If the limit is exceeded, return a snapshot. That is a controlled trade-off: the map redraws once instead of spending seconds reconstructing an obsolete trail. During a failure drill, I disconnect a test courier at sequence 410 and let the producer continue through 590 while the map is offline. When the client returns, the gateway should either return every event after 410 or explicitly send a snapshot whose cursor is at least 590. I then inject a duplicate 511, swap the order of 532 and 533, and advance the test clock past the retention boundary. The expected result is boring: duplicates are ignored, a gap requests recovery, and an expired cursor gets a snapshot. The drill catches a subtle race too: if the snapshot is read at 589 while event 590 is committed, the response must identify its cursor so the client can ask for 590 instead of silently losing that update. This is why I keep the recovery evaluator next to the service code; a dashboard showing connected sockets cannot prove correctness. Token scope belongs here too. A reconnect token should authorize one tenant and the specific delivery or map view, with an expiry shorter than the retention window. Authentication proves who is asking; the cursor proves what they already saw. They solve different problems. A practical decision rule An event replay path fits when events are small, the expected offline gap fits comfortably inside the retention window, and an exact trail matters. A snapshot path fits when a delivery has high update volume, viewers often return after long gaps, or the product only needs the current marker. A hybrid policy is usually the least surprising: replay a bounded number of events, then fall back to a snapshot with a clear cursor. The catch is that a short window is not suitable for forensic history, legal retention, or analytics that need every coordinate. Keep an append-only, access-controlled archive for those jobs, and keep the map log optimized for recovery. Stick with a queue that deletes acknowledged messages when you need simple task handoff; choose a replayable log when multiple consumers and deterministic backfill are requirements. No single retention number satisfies both. Before shipping, I run the same checks in the notebook and in CI: reconnect at each boundary, verify monotonic sequences, expire old records with a clock injected into tests, and load-test snapshot fallback. Then I review privacy language with product and security. The operational checklist is short: define the cursor contract, document expiry, cap replay work, record recovery metrics, and rehearse a shard restore. If any one of those is vague, the map is still relying on luck. References https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/ https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6455 https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110

title: Multiplayer Quiz Presence: Safe Realtime Channel Deletion in Python
author: ColeMitchell4991
summary: Short answer: treat channel deletion as a protocol state transition, not as a socket operation. Mark the quiz session closing, stop admitting messages, drain or reject late events, then close the peer connection only after the authoritative state is durable. A reconnecting player should receive a fresh session decision, never guess whether the old channel still exists. In a marketplace-style quiz, presence accuracy is the decision axis. A player can be shown as online while their answer is already irrelevant, or shown offline while a score update is still in flight. Both cases damage trust. The implementation below keeps the source of truth in a small state machine and makes every teardown request idempotent. How should a multiplayer quiz game handle realtime channel deletion? The data flow is deliberately boring. A Python worker owns the session record; a signaling layer exchanges WebRTC offers, answers, and ICE candidates; browsers carry quiz events over a data channel. The worker decides when a round ends or a host removes a player. It records that decision before asking the transport to close. WebRTC defines the peer connection and data-channel states, but your application still owns authorization, ordering, and replay policy. Here is a minimal controller using an in-memory store so the lifecycle is visible. In production, replace the store with a transactional database or a consensus-backed service. The transport adapter can wrap any WebRTC implementation. from dataclasses import dataclass , field from enum import Enum from threading import Lock from typing import Dict , Optional class ChannelState ( str , Enum ): OPEN = " open " CLOSING = " closing " CLOSED = " closed " @dataclass class QuizChannel : channel_id : str state : ChannelState = ChannelState . OPEN close_reason : Optional [ str ] = None seen_events : set [ str ] = field ( default_factory = set ) class ChannelRegistry : def __init__ ( self ) -> None : self . _channels : Dict [ str , QuizChannel ] = {} self . _lock = Lock () def create ( self , channel_id : str ) -> QuizChannel : with self . _lock : channel = self . _channels . setdefault ( channel_id , QuizChannel ( channel_id )) if channel . state is ChannelState . CLOSED : raise ValueError ( " channel_id belongs to a closed quiz session " ) return channel def accept_event ( self , channel_id : str , event_id : str ) -> bool : with self . _lock : channel = self . _channels . get ( channel_id ) if channel is None or channel . state is not ChannelState . OPEN : return False if event_id in channel . seen_events : return False channel . seen_events . add ( event_id ) return True def delete ( self , channel_id : str , reason : str ) -> bool : with self . _lock : channel = self . _channels . get ( channel_id ) if channel is None or channel . state is ChannelState . CLOSED : return False # An already-completed delete is a safe retry. channel . state = ChannelState . CLOSING channel . close_reason = reason return True def mark_closed ( self , channel_id : str ) -> None : with self . _lock : channel = self . _channels . get ( channel_id ) if channel is not None : channel . state = ChannelState . CLOSED The important ordering is OPEN -> CLOSING -> CLOSED . delete does not pretend that the network has already stopped; it changes the admission rule immediately. A message arriving between those two moments is rejected by accept_event , and a duplicate delete is harmless. The event ID is also the boundary between retry and replay: an answer processor can acknowledge an ID twice while applying its score once. Close twice. The second call should be boring. Keep transport shutdown outside the lock. After the state transition commits, notify the signaling service, call the peer connection's close() method, and publish a final presence update. If a process dies after the database commit but before close() , a sweeper can finish the transport work. If it dies before the commit, a retry sees OPEN and performs the same transition. That is the useful failure boundary. Failure paths that make presence lie The first failure is a half-delete: one browser receives a close event while another still has a sendable data channel. The server must reject events by state, not by what a client reports. Client-side readyState is helpful telemetry, not authorization. The second is a reconnect racing teardown. Give each session a monotonically increasing generation, or a random session incarnation ID. A reconnect presents its incarnation; an old close callback cannot mark the new incarnation offline. This prevents a delayed callback from erasing fresh presence. The third is a lost final notification. Presence should be derived from durable session state on read, with transport callbacks treated as hints. A periodic reconciliation job can compare active connections with OPEN records and close abandoned ones. Pick a timeout from observed network behavior and document it; I'm not sure one universal value exists across mobile networks. The fourth is a split brain between scoring and teardown. Store the round result and the close transition in one transaction when the rules require that atomicity. Otherwise, explicitly define which outcome wins and expose it in the audit trail. “The channel closed” is not an explanation for a missing score. A test matrix before shipping An eval-driven harness should exercise the state machine without a browser first, then add real peer connections for transport behavior. The matrix below is small enough to run on every change. Scenario Expected invariant Useful assertion Delete retried three times One durable transition Delete side effect has one audit record Event races with delete No post-close mutation Score version is unchanged after CLOSING Old reconnect arrives late New incarnation stays present Generation on the record is newest Worker crashes after commit Session is not admitted Sweeper eventually closes transport Duplicate answer event Exactly-once scoring Same event_id yields one score delta For a Python test, inject a fake transport and control the scheduler. Force the sequence delete commit -> process stop -> reconnect -> sweep ; randomize message arrival around each edge. For example, send answer evt-1042 just after the host's delete request, kill the worker before the browser sees close() , then let a reconnect present incarnation 8 while the stale callback still claims incarnation 7. The expected trace is explicit: evt-1042 is rejected, the old callback is ignored, and the sweeper moves the committed record from CLOSING to CLOSED . Record transition latency, rejected-event counts, and the age of CLOSING sessions. Those metrics tell you whether presence is stale, while logs with channel ID, incarnation, and event ID let you reconstruct a disputed round without storing answer content. Choosing the transport boundary WebRTC is a good fit when browsers need direct, low-latency data channels and your application already operates a signaling path. Its specification covers RTCPeerConnection , ICE negotiation, and data-channel lifecycle; it does not define your quiz authorization or durable event log. That division is healthy: keep game rules in Python and keep media or network mechanics behind an adapter. A server-relayed WebSocket path can be simpler for authoritative fan-out, especially when every answer must pass through one region. A WebRTC data channel can reduce relay work but introduces signaling, NAT traversal, and another set of connection states to observe. The right choice depends on where you need ordering and auditability. Do not select a transport from a latency chart alone. The catch is that this pattern is not suitable when you need a globally ordered, permanently replayable stream from the transport itself; use a durable log and treat the realtime channel as a view. Stick with a simpler server push path when your team cannot operate ICE and signaling diagnostics. That is an operational boundary, not a failure of the protocol. Before launch, write the deletion contract in one page: who may request it, which events are accepted in each state, how long CLOSING may last, and what a reconnect receives. Then run the matrix under packet delay, duplicate delivery, process restarts, and clock skew. Keep prompt payloads and telemetry lean if an AI agent is generating quiz content, but never remove event IDs or transition records to save tokens. Those fields pay for themselves during the first disputed score. References https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/ https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/RTCPeerConnection/close https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/RTCDataChannel/readyState

title: How to Evaluate a Copied Polymarket Trade in Python
author: Dexoryn
summary: A copy-trading bot should not assume that a trade is worth copying just because another wallet executed it. The source trader might have entered at a favorable price. By the time your bot detects the transaction, the market may have moved, the available liquidity may have changed, or the opportunity may no longer meet your strategy's requirements. The solution is to separate trade detection from trade evaluation. In this tutorial, we'll build a small Python component that evaluates a proposed copied trade using the follower's estimated entry price, probability estimate, and transaction costs. We'll also add tests for common rejection scenarios. The example is an educational model. It does not connect to a live wallet, submit orders, or establish that a strategy is profitable. Model the source trade and the follower's entry The source wallet's price is useful context, but the follower needs to make a decision using the price available when the follower intends to trade. Let's represent the relevant information with a Python dataclass. from dataclasses import dataclass from decimal import Decimal @dataclass(frozen=True) class CopyTradeCandidate: token_id: str source_price: Decimal follower_entry_price: Decimal estimated_probability: Decimal estimated_cost_per_share: Decimal Each field has a distinct role: "token_id" identifies the outcome token. "source_price" records the source wallet's observed entry price. "follower_entry_price" represents the follower's estimated executable purchase price. "estimated_probability" is the strategy's estimate of the outcome's probability of winning. "estimated_cost_per_share" represents estimated transaction costs per share. The source price and follower entry price should never be treated as interchangeable. For a real implementation, validate the token identifier against trusted market metadata and obtain price information from a current, reliable market-data source. Calculate the follower's expected value For a binary outcome share bought and held until resolution, a winning share pays $1 and a losing share pays $0. If the estimated probability of winning is (q), the entry price is (p), and the estimated cost per share is (c), the simplified expected value per share is: [ EV=q-p-c ] This calculation assumes the probability estimate is meaningful and that the purchase price represents the actual cost of acquiring a share, before the separately modeled costs. Implement it as follows: def expected_value_per_share( probability: Decimal, entry_price: Decimal, cost_per_share: Decimal, ) -> Decimal: if not Decimal("0") < probability < Decimal("1"): raise ValueError("Probability must be between 0 and 1") if not Decimal("0") < entry_price < Decimal("1"): raise ValueError("Entry price must be between 0 and 1") if cost_per_share < Decimal("0"): raise ValueError("Cost cannot be negative") return probability - entry_price - cost_per_share Using "Decimal" helps avoid binary floating-point representation issues in financial calculations. It does not make the probability estimate more accurate or remove uncertainty from the model. Compare the source price with the follower's price Consider this hypothetical example: Source entry price: $0.40 Follower's estimated entry price: $0.52 Estimated probability of winning: 60% Estimated cost per share: $0.01 The source's entry price and the follower's entry price produce different estimated values. For the follower: [ EV=0.60-0.52-0.01=$0.07 ] The estimated expected value is $0.07 per share under these assumptions. Now suppose the follower's entry price increases to $0.60: [ EV=0.60-0.60-0.01=-$0.01 ] The estimated expected value becomes negative. The source trade has not changed, but the follower's economics have changed. A copy-trading bot should not blindly reproduce the transaction when its own entry conditions are no longer satisfied. These figures are illustrative, not actual Polymarket market data or a forecast of returns. Implement a trade-evaluation function Now combine the calculation with a minimum expected-value threshold and a maximum acceptable price difference from the source trade. @dataclass(frozen=True) class EvaluationResult: approved: bool reason: str expected_value: Decimal | None def evaluate_copy_trade( candidate: CopyTradeCandidate, *, minimum_ev: Decimal, maximum_price_difference: Decimal, ) -> EvaluationResult: if not candidate.token_id: return EvaluationResult( False, "MISSING_TOKEN_ID", None ) if not ( Decimal("0") < candidate.source_price < Decimal("1") ): return EvaluationResult( False, "INVALID_SOURCE_PRICE", None ) price_difference = ( candidate.follower_entry_price - candidate.source_price ) if price_difference > maximum_price_difference: return EvaluationResult( False, "PRICE_MOVED_TOO_FAR", None ) ev = expected_value_per_share( candidate.estimated_probability, candidate.follower_entry_price, candidate.estimated_cost_per_share, ) if ev < minimum_ev: return EvaluationResult( False, "EXPECTED_VALUE_TOO_LOW", ev ) return EvaluationResult(True, "APPROVED", ev) This example focuses on a BUY trade, where a higher follower entry price is less favorable. A production implementation should validate all inputs, explicitly handle supported trade directions, and model costs according to the applicable fee schedule. The price-difference rule is also strategy-specific. A price increase does not automatically make a trade unattractive, and a small price difference does not automatically make it worthwhile. The expected-value check remains necessary. Before using this function in production, add explicit checks for probability bounds, entry-price bounds, negative costs, and any other invalid input states. Test the decision logic A copy-trading decision should be testable without submitting a real order. The following pytest tests cover a candidate that meets the example thresholds and one that exceeds the permitted price difference. from decimal import Decimal def make_candidate( overrides): values = { "token_id": "example-token", "source_price": Decimal("0.40"), "follower_entry_price": Decimal("0.42"), "estimated_probability": Decimal("0.60"), "estimated_cost_per_share": Decimal("0.01"), } values.update(overrides) return CopyTradeCandidate( values) def test_approves_candidate_with_sufficient_edge(): result = evaluate_copy_trade( make_candidate(), minimum_ev=Decimal("0.05"), maximum_price_difference=Decimal("0.05"), ) assert result.approved is True assert result.reason == "APPROVED" def test_rejects_excessive_price_movement(): result = evaluate_copy_trade( make_candidate( follower_entry_price=Decimal("0.50") ), minimum_ev=Decimal("0.05"), maximum_price_difference=Decimal("0.05"), ) assert result.approved is False assert result.reason == "PRICE_MOVED_TOO_FAR" Save the implementation and tests in separate files, importing the relevant classes and functions, then run: pip install pytest pytest -q These tests check the intended behavior of the example. They do not test live order-book data, order submission, or actual profitability. A fuller test suite should cover invalid inputs, stale market data, missing tokens, insufficient expected value, exposure limits, and price changes immediately before execution. Use current market data for the follower's price A real copy-trading system needs to retrieve market data for the specific outcome token it intends to trade. Polymarket's "official data guide" ( https://institute.polymarket.com/data ) documents public market-data access, including retrieving token prices and historical prices. For a practical integration, the bot should: Identify the correct outcome token from the observed transaction. Retrieve current market data for that token. Estimate the executable price for the intended order quantity. Apply the strategy's price and expected-value checks. Revalidate the order constraints before execution when necessary. The best available ask may not represent the average price for a large order. A production system may need to inspect multiple ask levels to estimate the cost of filling the intended quantity. Market data can also change between retrieval and submission. The execution layer should enforce appropriate price limits rather than assuming that the previously observed price remains available. Keep evaluation separate from execution The evaluation function should decide whether a candidate meets the strategy's requirements. It should not sign or submit orders itself. A safer architecture separates the responsibilities: Monitor: Detects relevant source-wallet activity. Normalizer: Converts observed activity into a validated trade candidate. Market-data service: Retrieves current prices and order-book information. Evaluator: Applies price, expected-value, and risk rules. Execution service: Handles order submission and order-state reconciliation. Logger: Records decisions, rejection reasons, and execution outcomes. This structure makes failures easier to investigate. For example, if a bot repeatedly rejects copied trades because prices have moved too far, the logs can help establish whether the issue is detection latency, slow processing, or a strategy threshold that needs review. If an order submission times out, the execution service should reconcile the order's status before retrying. Otherwise, a retry could duplicate an order that was already accepted. Conclusion Copying a transaction is not the same as copying the opportunity. A useful copy-trading system evaluates the follower's own entry price, estimated probability, costs, and risk constraints before deciding whether to act. The Python example in this tutorial demonstrates how to isolate that decision logic and test it independently of live trading infrastructure. It is a foundation for further development, not a complete production bot. The next engineering steps are to integrate reliable market data, model executable prices for the intended order size, add portfolio risk controls, and test execution failure scenarios. title: How to scrape Glassdoor jobs and salaries into Excel or Python (no login, no API key)
author: Norbert Sobala
summary: Glassdoor is one of the few job boards that shows a salary range next to the job : either the employer's own or a Glassdoor estimate. It also shows the company rating . That makes the data useful beyond job hunting. Two common uses: Salary benchmarking. What do product managers in Berlin actually get offered? Sales and recruiting. Which companies are hiring right now, and for which roles? A company opening five sales positions this month is usually a company with budget. Glassdoor has no public API for this, and logged-out visitors only see the first page of results. This guide uses a ready-made scraper on Apify that handles both problems. You can get the data without writing any code, or call it from Python. What you get Every job comes back as one clean record: Field Example title Product Manager (m/w/d) company Lokalleads GmbH location / country Berlin, Germany salaryMin / salaryMax 60000 / 60000 salaryCurrency / salaryPeriod EUR / year salaryIsEstimate false (set by the employer, not a Glassdoor estimate) salaryYearlyMinEur 60000 (normalised to EUR per year, so you can compare countries) remote hybrid easyApply true postedAt 2026-10-14 You can also turn on: Full descriptions , which add the whole job text, employment type and industry. Company signals , which add one summary record per company: open roles, jobs posted in the last 7 days, remote share and median salary. This is handy for spotting companies that are scaling up. Option 1: no code (2 minutes) Open Glassdoor Jobs Scraper and click Try for free . Type your search, e.g. product manager , choose a location ( Berlin ) and a country. Optionally tick Only jobs with salary , Remote only , or a date range such as Posted in the last 7 days . Click Start . When the run finishes, export to Excel, CSV or JSON , or send the data straight to Google Sheets. When we ran "product manager" in Berlin , 10 jobs came back in under a minute. Two of them had a salary published by the employer: €60,000 and €72,000 a year. The employers ranged from small agencies to Bundesdruckerei and Berliner Sparkasse. How many listings carry a salary depends on the country. Several US states require pay ranges in job ads, so US searches usually return far more numbers than German ones. If you only want listings with pay, tick Only jobs with salary . Option 2: Python pip install apify-client pandas from apify_client import ApifyClient import pandas as pd client = ApifyClient ( " YOUR_APIFY_TOKEN " ) # Console → Settings → API & Integrations run = client . actor ( " liveclaude/glassdoor-jobs-scraper " ). call ( run_input = { " searchQueries " : [ " data analyst " , " data engineer " ], " locations " : [ " London " ], " country " : " gb " , " postedWithin " : " week " , " onlyWithSalary " : True , " maxJobsPerSearch " : 200 , }) jobs = list ( client . dataset ( run [ " defaultDatasetId " ]). iterate_items ()) df = pd . DataFrame ( jobs ) # median advertised salary per search, in EUR per year print ( df . groupby ( " searchQuery " )[[ " salaryYearlyMinEur " , " salaryYearlyMaxEur " ]]. median ()) df . to_excel ( " glassdoor_jobs.xlsx " , index = False ) The salaryYearlyMinEur and salaryYearlyMaxEur fields are already converted to euros per year. That lets you compare London with Sydney or New York without converting anything yourself. Keep it fresh automatically Add a Schedule in Apify, for example every Monday at 8:00, and turn on Only new jobs . Each run then returns only listings you haven't seen before. From there you can push new jobs to Slack or email as alerts, or append them to a Google Sheet and keep a running salary tracker. Make, Zapier and n8n work too if you want the data in a CRM. What does it cost? You pay per result: $0.50 per 1,000 jobs , and $3 per 1,000 if you also want full descriptions. Platform costs are included. A weekly tracker of a few hundred jobs costs cents. Apify's free plan includes monthly credit, which is enough to try it. A note on responsible use The scraper collects only what Glassdoor shows publicly to logged-out visitors. It does not log in and does not collect reviews written by individuals. If you store data about people (for example, recruiters' names in descriptions), treat it according to GDPR or your local law. Questions or a missing field? Open an issue on the Actor page . Requests usually ship within a few days. This tutorial was written with AI assistance and checked by the author. All numbers come from a real run of the scraper.

title: MBA Capstone Modeling: How to Fix Heteroscedasticity and HC3 Robust Standard Errors in OLS in Python Before Defense
author: Python_MBA_Analytics
summary: MBA Capstone Modeling: How to Fix Heteroscedasticity and HC3 Robust Standard Errors in OLS in Python Before Defense Introduction 📌 Urgent Thesis & Dissertation Support: If you need assistance resolving statistical package errors or preparing compliant data chapters, vetted academic specialists at EssayMarket provide 1-on-1 code reviews and custom reporting. In MBA capstone projects, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression is the default statistical tool for predicting financial metrics such as revenue, cost of goods sold, or stock volatility. However, a critical failure point occurs when the assumption of homoscedasticity is violated. Heteroscedasticity—where the variance of error terms is not constant across all levels of an independent variable—invalidates the standard errors, t-statistics, and p-values generated by standard OLS output. Many students rely on default outputs from statistical packages like SPSS or basic Python functions (e.g., statsmodels.OLS.fit() ). These tools report "naive" standard errors that assume constant variance. When this assumption is violated, which is common in financial data due to scale effects (e.g., larger firms having larger absolute sales errors), the model’s inference becomes unreliable. Professors often reject these models during defense because the confidence intervals are biased, leading to incorrect conclusions about variable significance. While some packages offer robust standard errors by default, others require explicit specification. This guide details how to detect heteroscedasticity and implement HC3 (Heteroscedasticity Consistent) robust standard errors in Python to ensure your model’s statistical validity. Step-by-Step Fix / Walkthrough The correction process involves two phases: detection and adjustment. Phase 1: Detecting Heteroscedasticity in Python First, fit the baseline OLS model. We use statsmodels because it provides direct access to residual diagnostics. import statsmodels.api as sm import pandas as pd import numpy as np # Load data data = pd . read_csv ( ' financial_data.csv ' ) # Define variables # X: Independent variables (e.g., Marketing Spend, R&D) # y: Dependent variable (e.g., Revenue) X = data [[ ' marketing_spend ' , ' rd_expense ' ]] y = data [ ' revenue ' ] # Add constant term X = sm . add_constant ( X ) # Fit baseline OLS model_ols = sm . OLS ( y , X ). fit () print ( model_ols . summary ()) To test for heteroscedasticity, use the Breusch-Pagan Test or the White Test . The Breusch-Pagan test is standard for MBA-level work. # Perform Breusch-Pagan Test # The test statistic follows a chi-square distribution bp_test = sm . stats . diagnostic . het_breuschpagan ( model_ols . resid , model_ols . model . exog ) # bp_test[0] is the LM statistic # bp_test[1] is the p-value print ( f " Breusch-Pagan LM Statistic: { bp_test [ 0 ] : . 4 f } " ) print ( f " Breusch-Pagan P-Value: { bp_test [ 1 ] : . 4 f } " ) Interpretation: If the p-value is less than 0.05, you reject the null hypothesis of homoscedasticity. In this case, standard errors are invalid, and robust standard errors are required. Phase 2: Implementing HC3 Robust Standard Errors HC3 is preferred over HC1 or HC2 in small-to-medium sample sizes because it provides a finite-sample correction that is less likely to produce negative variance estimates. It adjusts the covariance matrix of the parameter estimates using the leverage values of the observations. # Fit the model with HC3 robust covariance # cov_type='HC3' specifies the heteroscedasticity-consistent estimator model_robust = sm . OLS ( y , X ). fit ( cov_type = ' HC3 ' ) # Print summary to compare with baseline print ( model_robust . summary ()) Key Parameters Explained: cov_type='HC3' : This flag instructs statsmodels to calculate the sandwich estimator for the covariance matrix. The "3" denotes the specific correction formula: $V = (X'X)^{-1} ( \sum u_i^2 (1 - h_{ii})^{-2} x_i x_i' ) (X'X)^{-1}$, where $h_{ii}$ is the leverage of observation $i$. use_t=True : By default, statsmodels uses the t-distribution for p-values when degrees of freedom are limited. Ensure this is enabled for accurate p-values in smaller datasets (< 1000 observations). ⚡ Pro Tip: If your department rubric requires custom econometric adjustments that standard packages don't output cleanly, consulting with a verified data modeling specialist saves weeks of defense delays. Practical Data Example & APA 7 Reporting The following table compares the baseline OLS output with the HC3 Robust output for a hypothetical model predicting Revenue based on Marketing and R&D . Note the significant change in the p-value for R&D , which becomes statistically significant only after accounting for heteroscedasticity. Variable Coef (OLS) Std. Err. (OLS) P-Value (OLS) Coef (HC3) Std. Err. (HC3) P-Value (HC3) Intercept 12.45 3.20 0.002 12.45 4.15 0.041 Marketing 1.85 0.45 0.000 1.85 0.62 0.000 R&D 0.92 0.50 0.073 0.92 0.38 0.021 R-squared 0.65 0.65 Adj. R-squared 0.64 0.64 Note: Coefficients remain identical; only standard errors and subsequent inferential statistics change. APA 7 Reporting Format When reporting these results in your capstone paper, you must explicitly state the use of robust standard errors. Do not report the naive standard errors. Example Text: "A multiple linear regression was conducted to predict revenue from marketing spend and R&D expense. The Breusch-Pagan test indicated significant heteroscedasticity, $\chi^2(2) = 15.42, p < .001$. Consequently, heteroscedasticity-consistent (HC3) robust standard errors were used to ensure valid inference. The analysis revealed that marketing spend was a significant predictor of revenue ($B = 1.85$, 95% CI [1.20, 2.50], $p < .001$). R&D expense also emerged as a significant predictor when robust standard errors were applied ($B = 0.92$, 95% CI [0.16, 1.68], $p = .021$). The model explained 65% of the variance in revenue ($R^2 = .65$, $F(2, 97) = 92.5, p < .001$)." Common Pitfalls & What to Check Confusing Corrected vs. Raw Standard Errors: In statsmodels , params (coefficients) do not change with cov_type . Only bse , tvalues , and pvalues change. Ensure you are extracting the correct arrays for reporting. Small Sample Sizes: HC3 is robust, but if $N < 30$, the t-distribution approximation may still be weak. Consider using the use_t=True parameter and acknowledging small sample limitations in your discussion. Multicollinearity Interaction: Heteroscedasticity does not cause bias in coefficients, but multicollinearity does. Run the Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) test before interpreting coefficients. If VIF > 10, address multicollinearity first, as robust standard errors will not fix unstable coefficient estimates. Outliers: HC3 downweights the influence of high-leverage points (via the $1 - h_{ii}$ term), but extreme outliers can still distort results. Perform a residual plot check ( model_robust.plot_leverage ) to identify and justify the exclusion or retention of influential points. Software Default Settings: In R, lm() does not use robust SEs by default; you must use the sandwich package. In Python, statsmodels requires explicit cov_type specification. In SPSS, you must go to Analyze > Regression > Linear > Options > Statistics and check "Robust Standard Errors." Relying on default GUI outputs is a frequent cause of rejection. Conclusion / Next Steps Heteroscedasticity is a common feature in financial and business data due to scale effects. Ignoring it leads to invalid hypothesis tests and a weak capstone defense. By explicitly testing for this violation using the Breusch-Pagan test and applying HC3 robust standard errors in Python, you ensure that your p-values and confidence intervals are statistically defensible. Add a methodological note in your appendix detailing the Breusch-Pagan test results and the rationale for selecting HC3 over HC1 or HC2. title: Secret sauce code now open source ( * it beats AI generated code)
author: tdk-cli
summary:
TDK CLI: How a Simple service.json Becomes a Full Local Stack Most multi-service setups still force you to maintain Docker Compose files, Tiltfiles, nginx configs, port maps, and health checks by hand. AI coding agents make the application code easy, but they are still bad at keeping the local infrastructure consistent. TDK CLI solves this by treating a tiny declarative file as the source of truth and generating everything else. The Contract This is essentially all you write for a service: { "$schema" : "https://tdk-landscape.github.io/schema.service.json" , "schemaVersion" : 1 , "appName" : "orders-api" , "appType" : "backend" , "stack" : "shop" , "port" : 4000 , "healthCheckPath" : "/health" , "dependsOn" : [] } From this single file, TDK generates Dockerfiles, live-reload rules, Traefik routes, shared Postgres wiring, health probes, and the Tilt configuration that actually runs it. The project is organized as Project → Stack → Resource . flowchart LR P[Project
.tdk/project.json] --> S1[Stack: shop] P --> S2[Stack: billing] S1 --> R1[orders-api
backend] S1 --> R2[orders-app
frontend] S2 --> R3[checkout-api
backend] Three Subsystems The codebase is deliberately split so each part has a clear job: flowchart TB subgraph CLI["cli/ (TypeScript)"] Commands[Commands & validation] Templates[Handlebars templates] Ports[Port allocation] end subgraph Discovery["discovery/ (Starlark)"] Scan[Scan service.json] DAG[Build dependency DAG] end subgraph Engine["engine/ (Starlark)"] LiveUpdate[live_update rules] Traefik[Traefik routing] Infra[Postgres + platform] end CLI -->|generates Tiltfile + configs| Discovery Discovery -->|registry + DAG| Engine Engine -->|docker_build + containers| Docker[(Docker)] Subsystem Language Responsibility cli/ TypeScript Commands, validation, port allocation, template generation, launching Tilt discovery/ Starlark Scan for service.json files, normalize them, build the dependency DAG engine/ Starlark Runs inside Tilt — turns the DAG into real docker_build , live_update , Traefik, Postgres, etc. The CLI never starts containers itself. The engine never parses CLI flags. Discovery never builds images. The Generation Step The real glue is the template engine ( cli/src/generator/template-engine.ts ). It reads .tdk/project.json and emits files into the gitignored .tdk/.tdk-out/ directory: Tiltfile TILT_TECH_STACK.star and TILT_RESOURCE_DEFAULTS.star spec.master .tiltignore These come from Handlebars templates.
