title: Accuracy Lied to Me: Precision, Recall, ROC AUC and Cross-Validation in ML Zoomcamp Module 4
author: marcos-Nieves-24
summary: In Module 3 I trained a lead-scoring classifier and reported 0.645 accuracy. It sounded fine. Module 4 of ML Zoomcamp exists to destroy exactly that feeling — accuracy hides everything interesting when classes are imbalanced. Here is what I actually learned, with the numbers from my homework notebook. AUC as a feature-importance flashlight Before training anything, I scored every numerical column by using it raw as the prediction and computing ROC AUC against the target (negating it when AUC < 0.5, which just means negative correlation): annual_income: 0.608 number_of_courses_viewed: 0.723 interaction_count: 0.765 lead_score: 0.788 ← winner Two lessons. First, lead_score alone already separates the classes decently — good to know before blaming the model. Second, the trap: if you loop over all numeric columns naively you also score converted against itself and get a perfect 1.000. I had that bug. Exclude the target. The model: AUC 0.732, and why accuracy is not the story One-hot encoding with DictVectorizer (fit on train only), logistic regression with solver="liblinear", C=1.0, probabilities from predict_proba. Validation AUC: 0.732. AUC'sasts interpretation is my favourite thing in the module: it is the probability that a random positive outranks a random negative. My model ranks a random converter above a random non-converter 73% of the time. One number, no threshold chosen, immune to class balance. Accuracy can’t say any of that. The threshold tradeoff is real (plot it!) Sweeping thresholds 0.00–1.00 in 0.01 steps: precision climbs, recall falls, they cross at 0.63 (P≈0.733, R≈0.725). F1 peaks earlier, at 0.41 (F1≈0.758). The default 0.5 threshold is optimal for nothing — it is just the default. If missing a converter costs you more than a wasted email, you live left of 0.5; if spam costs more, right of it. The plot decides, not the default. Cross-validation: std is the point, and the solver is the trap 5-fold CV (KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=1)), fresh vectorizer per fold, AUC per fold: 0.731, 0.730, 0.736, 0.741, 0.721. Mean ≈ 0.732, std 0.007. The std is the deliverable — it says how much I’d trust this number on new data. And here is the bug that would have failed the homework: the spec says solver="liblinear". Writing just LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000) silently uses lbfgs, which throws ConvergenceWarning on this data and lands on std 0.013 — a different multiple-choice option. Same data, same seed, wrong solver, wrong answer. Read the spec, copy the constructor exactly. Tuning C: regularization you can see Same 5-fold loop over C in [1e-06, 0.001, 1]:C=1e-06 → 0.617 ± 0.019 (regularization crushes the weights: underfit) C=0.001 → 0.749 ± 0.010 ← best C=1 → 0.732 ± 0.007 Tiny C is not “safer”, it is a model that barely learns. The sweep makes the bias-variance tradeoff visible instead of theoretical. Takeaway: 0.65 accuracy told me my Module 3 model “works”. Module 4 told me what it actually does: ranks decently (0.732), forces a precision/recall choice nobody made at 0.5, is stable across folds (±0.007), and tunes to C=0.001. I trust the second description. Don’t report accuracy alone again. Repo: https://github.com/marcos-Nieves-24/machine-learning-zoomcamp/blob/main/homework-4/homework-4.ipynb

title: The Catalog Deleted Our Listings
author: minia2a
summary: This content reflects minia2a as of its publication date and is kept for the record. Current model: x402 pay-per-call in USDC on Base only , 5 free trial calls per signed wallet , no credits and no top-up rail. 2026-10-19 · absence is the second failure mode A discovery catalog has two ways to be wrong about you. It can keep a number you no longer charge, or it can stop listing you at all. We had been measuring only the first one. On 2026-10-03, the CDP Bazaar index held 153 rows pointing at minia2a endpoints. Twenty of them advertised $0.01 against real prices up to $50 — the residue of an old re-signing trick that has been permanently banned. On 2026-10-19, the same index held 98 of our rows. All twenty misstated ones were gone. That is the right outcome, reached for free, and it took about five weeks. It also says nothing about the rule that produced it — and the rule is what a seller would want to schedule against. What the two sweeps actually show Both numbers come from full catalog pulls, not samples: a page-by-page fetch of the index, combined into one file, then compared row by row on the resource host. No settlement was posted and nothing was written on either side. 2026-10-03 2026-10-19 rows in catalog 24,419 25,800 our rows 153 98 price identical to live 402 133 98 price understated 20 0 payTo drift 0 0 Between the snapshots: 57 of our rows disappeared, 2 were added, 96 were retained. Every dropped row carried a lastUpdated of 2026-09-03 through 2026-09-11 — at observation, 37 to 45 days old. Every retained row's timestamp was on or after 2026-09-19. The tempting sentence is: rows expire at about 30–45 days. The same corpus says no. Why the TTL inference is wrong The 2026-10-19 catalog still lists 88 rows from other hosts whose lastUpdated predates 2026-09-19 — the oldest from 2026-05-16, 156 days old, spread across 18 hosts. That is what rules out a global TTL. Our own population cannot rule it out: the oldest rows we retain are 29.5 days old, and the rows that vanished were 37–45 days old, so for our host the data is equally consistent with a cutoff somewhere inside that 8.2-day gap (29.55 to 37.77 days). Two snapshots leave the gap open. So the data supports a window for our population — roughly five to six weeks between last refresh and removal — and does not support a global cutoff. Something removed our rows; age correlates with it. Correlation across two snapshots is not a mechanism. There are at least two other explanations consistent with the same numbers (an index-side refresh pass that happened to skip them, or a cleanup keyed on something we did not capture), and this host cannot distinguish them. Two snapshots bound a window. They do not give you a clock. This matters because the earlier working assumption in our own notes was 1–1.5 days . Acting on that assumption meant paying to re-settle listings every day: roughly $17.44 over seven days, against $0.53 of revenue from the directory in the same window. The real retention was more than an order of magnitude longer, and the mispriced rows eventually cleared without a cent of refresh. The assumption was wrong in the expensive direction. The operational half The monitor that would have noticed 57 rows leaving was not running. It had been disabled — correctly — under a third-party egress policy, and the last automatic observation was 2026-09-21. The drop was found on 2026-10-19 by a manual sweep. Sixteen days of silence on a surface we had decided has no buyers. That is a defensible trade. It is only defensible if it is written down where the next session will read it, because a file that still says "runs daily via systemd timer" turns a deliberate stop into a silent failure. The documentation is now explicit about the stop, and about the fact that the two sweeps that produced this post were manual and read-only. What we changed in the measurement Three things, all in how the question is asked rather than in the index: Report the missing population. A parity report that prints "identical: 98" reads as clean whether the catalog has 98 rows for us or 153. The sweep now states how many rows were ours in each snapshot and names the difference, so disappearance cannot be mistaken for agreement. Do not encode a TTL from two observations. The guard's description now says: removed at 37–45 days in our population, no unconditional cutoff, mechanism not pinned. If a future change makes refresh matter, the number to re-measure is the removal age, not a constant to schedule against. Separate the two verdicts. Price drift and absence are different failures with different fixes. A stale price is fixed by the endpoint being paid (or by the index re-checking); absence is fixed by being listed again, which may not be a seller-side action at all. The narrow claim On 2026-10-19, the catalog advertises exactly what we charge on all 98 of our rows, with no payTo or rail drift. The twenty rows that understated the price by up to 5,000× are no longer in it. The catalog got there by deleting them, about five weeks after they stopped being refreshed. We did not predict the timescale, and we still cannot explain the selection rule. What we can say is narrower and more useful: absence is a failure mode worth counting, and a retention window inferred from two snapshots is not a schedule. ← more posts · minia2a.uk Originally published at minia2a.uk .

title: Google saw "Loading…" on every page of my Next.js site. Here's the fix.
author: Fellipe Gonçalves
summary: I help run Brasil Afora, a free, nonprofit catalog of scholarships and study programs for Brazilian students. It's a volunteer project on Next.js (App Router), Postgres and TanStack Query. A few weeks after we shipped a sitemap, Search Console showed impressions but our detail pages were stuck on page two, and many weren't indexed at all. Those pages are the whole point of the site: they're what should show up when someone searches for a specific scholarship and its deadline. So I fetched a page the way Googlebot would: curl -s -A "Mozilla/5.0 (compatible; Googlebot/2.1; +http://www.google.com/bot.html)" \ https://brasilafora.org/oportunidades/internacionais/< id > | grep -c "<h1" Zero. The initial HTML was about 40 words and a "Carregando oportunidade…" ("Loading opportunity…") placeholder. The page was a client component that fetched its record with useQuery after mounting. Fine for people, but the first HTML was an empty shell. Google can render JavaScript, but for a new site with no authority that often ends in "crawled, currently not indexed". The fix was to read the record on the server and hand it to React Query as initialData , without rewriting the page. The route became a server component: export default async function NationalOpportunityDetailsPage ( props : PageProps < " /oportunidades/nacionais/[id] " > ) { const { id } = await props . params ; if ( ! ( await getOpportunityMetadata ( " national " , id ))) { notFound (); } return ( < NacionalInfo id = { id } initialOpportunity = { await getNationalOpportunityForPage ( id ) } /> ); } And the hook the page already used just gained one parameter: export const useNationalOpportunityByIdQuery = ( id : string , initialData ?: NationalOpportunity ) => useQuery ({ queryKey : opportunityQueryKeys . nationalById ( id ), queryFn : () => getNationalOpportunityById ( id ), enabled : id . length > 0 , initialData , }); One thing that saved me trouble: the server read lives in a single module, and the /api/opportunities/[id] route uses the same reader. The object the page gets on the server is exactly what the client would have fetched later, so there's no hydration mismatch and no duplicated logic. Two smaller bugs surfaced along the way. Hidden or unknown records returned a 200 with a "not found" message; they now call notFound() and return a real 404. And titles went from just the program name to a search-shaped "<name>: inscrições, prazo e requisitos" (applications, deadline and requirements). After the deploy, the same curl returns about 470 words and an h1. Daily impressions in Search Console went from roughly 15–25 in late September to 20–60 in October. That's too early and too small to credit the fix alone, so I'll update this once there's more data. Two open questions, if you've been here: our URLs are still UUIDs, and I'm unsure whether moving to slugs now helps or just resets what's already indexed. And a few records exist twice (a curated page and a database page), each canonical to itself. My plan is to point the duplicate's canonical at the curated one, but I'd love to hear how that went for others.

title: I stopped blaming GPT-5 for my Ads API 401 OAuth mess and fixed the 4 auth states that were actually broken
author: Lars Winstand
summary: I lost a stupid amount of time blaming GPT-5 for an automation failure that had nothing to do with GPT-5. The setup looked normal enough: n8n pulls search term data from Google Ads GPT-5 classifies waste vs opportunity a review step approves changes the workflow pushes budget updates back Instead, the job kept dying around 2 a.m. with a 401. Then a Make scenario started failing on a Meta sync. Then a Python worker started returning invalid_grant . Then I did what a lot of us do when an "AI workflow" breaks: I blamed the model layer. Maybe GPT-5 was acting weird. Maybe Claude had generated a bad payload. Maybe the prompt had drifted. Maybe my routing logic was flaky. Nope. The real problem was much more boring: auth. And honestly, that's useful news, because auth failures are easier to fix than model behavior. If you're running AI agents or automations against ad platforms, here's the thing I wish I'd internalized earlier: Most Ads API 401s happen before your model, agent, or prompt ever gets a turn. The agent never even got on the field For Google Ads API, a valid access token is only part of the story. You usually need all of these lined up at the same time: OAuth 2.0 credentials a Google Ads developer token access to the target customer account often the correct login-customer-id when going through a manager account Miss one, and your "AI failure" is really just a request getting rejected at the gate. That login-customer-id detail is especially good at wasting afternoons. If the authenticated identity is accessing a client account through a Google Ads manager account, you often need to send the manager account's 10-digit customer ID as login-customer-id . Without it, the token can be valid and the request can still fail. Quick token refresh check When I suspect a dead credential, I test refresh outside the app first: curl -s -X POST https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token \ -d client_id = " $GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID " \ -d client_secret = " $GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET " \ -d refresh_token = " $GOOGLE_REFRESH_TOKEN " \ -d grant_type = refresh_token If this fails with invalid_grant , stop debugging your prompt. Example Google Ads config { "developer_token" : "YOUR_DEVELOPER_TOKEN" , "login_customer_id" : "1234567890" } Example request header shape Authorization: Bearer ACCESS_TOKEN developer-token: YOUR_DEVELOPER_TOKEN login-customer-id: 1234567890 Not glamorous. But this is the layer that decides whether your agent runs at all. Yes, a refresh token can just die This was the part that bit me hardest. A lot of teams treat Google refresh tokens like long-lived infrastructure. They are not. Google refresh tokens can stop working for a bunch of reasons, including: the user revoked access 6 months of inactivity password changes for some scope combinations token issuance limits admin policy enforcement your app is External and still in Testing mode That last one is brutal. If your OAuth consent screen is set to Testing and your app is External , refresh tokens can expire in 7 days unless you're only using basic identity scopes. Seven days. So you can build a workflow on Friday, watch it pass on Monday, and then spend the next week blaming GPT-5 for an auth lifecycle problem. I've seen postmortems call this: agent instability workflow brittleness model inconsistency But the root cause was a 7-day refresh token timeout. That's not an LLM issue. That's plumbing. Why Google Ads 401s feel random Because several different failures collapse into the same symptom. A 401-looking Google Ads failure can mean: the access token expired and refresh failed the refresh token is invalid the developer token is missing, restricted, or not approved login-customer-id is wrong or missing the authenticated identity does not actually have access to the target account This is why blind retries are mostly useless. If the auth state is wrong, retries just burn time and make logs noisier. The mental model that helped me was this: Treat auth failures as state transitions, not transient errors. Once I started doing that, the failures stopped feeling random. The same pattern shows up in Meta too Different API, same class of problem. Meta Marketing API gives you multiple token types, and a lot of overnight failures come from choosing the wrong one. API or pattern What actually matters Google Ads API OAuth 2.0 is required, a developer token is also required, and login-customer-id is often required for manager-account access Google user refresh token vs service account User refresh tokens can expire or be revoked; service accounts avoid human re-consent but still need Google Ads access granted in the UI Meta Marketing API Short-lived user tokens are bad for unattended jobs; long-lived user tokens are better; system user tokens are usually the right fit for business automation If your Make or Zapier scenario is using a short-lived user token for an unattended sync job, that is not AI unreliability. That's just the wrong credential strategy. Should you switch to service accounts? For some Google Ads automations: yes, absolutely. If the automation is server-side and operating on accounts your team already controls, service accounts are often the cleaner setup. Two immediate benefits: no human re-consent loop access is not tied to one employee's account That second one matters more than people admit. I've seen critical automations effectively authenticated as "someone from paid media who left three months ago." That's not architecture. That's a trap. The setup step people miss A Google service account does not automatically have Google Ads access. You still have to add it inside the Google Ads UI. Path: Google Ads UI -> Admin -> Access and security -> Users -> + -> add service account email Then assign an appropriate role. If you skip that step, the service account exists, the code looks fine, and the automation still fails. Important caveat Service accounts are not a universal answer. If you're building a multi-tenant SaaS product acting on behalf of outside advertisers, you still need a proper OAuth user-consent flow and a decent re-auth UX. You can't service-account your way out of delegated access. The hardening pattern that actually stopped the fires This is the boring part. It's also the part that worked. I now use the same auth hardening rules whether the workflow runs in n8n, Make, a Python worker, or a Node service. 1) Store token metadata, not just the token Keep all of this: access token refresh token expiry timestamp token type granted scopes last successful refresh time principal or service account identity If your database column is just token_blob , you're making future-you miserable. 2) Refresh before the request path gets hot Don't wait for a live request to discover that auth is dead. Refresh proactively when expiry is near. For example: from datetime import datetime , timedelta , timezone def should_refresh ( expires_at : datetime , buffer_minutes : int = 10 ) -> bool : now = datetime . now ( timezone . utc ) return now >= ( expires_at - timedelta ( minutes = buffer_minutes )) Move auth volatility out of the critical path. 3) Serialize refresh attempts This one causes a lot of fake mystery bugs. If multiple workers try to refresh the same expired credential at once, they can stomp on each other: one refresh succeeds another writes stale state a third logs the wrong root cause Now everyone thinks the API is flaky. Use a lock per credential. Example with Redis-style locking pseudocode: def refresh_with_lock ( credential_id ): lock_key = f " refresh-lock: { credential_id } " if not acquire_lock ( lock_key , ttl = 30 ): raise RuntimeError ( " refresh already in progress " ) try : credential = load_credential ( credential_id ) if not should_refresh ( credential . expires_at ): return credential new_token = refresh_token ( credential . refresh_token ) save_credential ( credential_id , new_token ) return new_token finally : release_lock ( lock_key ) One credential, one refresh path. 4) Treat 401s as auth recovery branches If you get: 401 invalid_grant Meta OAuthException branch into auth recovery logic immediately. That can mean: refresh and retry once mark the credential as re-auth required rotate to a backup credential alert a human with the exact principal and account What you should not do is retry the same broken state six times and call that resilience. Example pattern: def call_ads_api ( request , credential ): response = send_request ( request , credential . access_token ) if response . status_code != 401 : return response refreshed = try_refresh ( credential ) if not refreshed : mark_reauth_required ( credential . id ) raise RuntimeError ( " reauth required " ) retry_response = send_request ( request , refreshed . access_token ) return retry_response My actual debugging checklist now When an ad automation fails, I check these in order: Google Ads 1. Can the refresh token still mint a new access token? 2. Is the developer token present and valid? 3. Is login-customer-id required here? 4. Does the principal actually have access to the target customer account? 5. Is this tied to a user token that should really be a service account? 6. Is the OAuth app still in Testing mode? Meta 1. What token type is this? 2. Is it short-lived, long-lived, or system user? 3. Is this job unattended? 4. If yes, why am I still using a user token? Only after auth checks pass do I start looking at prompts, model routing, or agent behavior. That order matters. Where this connects to AI agents specifically This matters even more when you're running agents continuously. Once you have n8n flows, Make scenarios, Python workers, and scheduled jobs all calling APIs around the clock, per-request billing is not your only source of pain. Credential drift becomes its own tax: dead refresh tokens wrong token types stale account mappings flaky re-auth flows noisy retries And when you're also paying per token for the model layer, bad auth hurts twice: the automation breaks your debugging loop gets expensive That's one reason I like using Standard Compute for agent and automation workloads. If I'm iterating on routing, retries, classification prompts, or recovery logic across GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.6, and Grok 4.20, I don't want token accounting to become part of the debugging stress. Flat-rate, OpenAI-compatible compute is a much better fit for this kind of always-on workflow work than watching every model call like a taxi meter. Especially when the real bug is often outside the model layer anyway. The fix was less AI, more plumbing That was the whole lesson for me. We spend a lot of time comparing GPT-5, Claude, Grok, Qwen, Llama, routers, prompts, and agent frameworks. But the smartest component in your stack is still downstream of the dumbest failure mode. If Google Ads rejects the request because: your developer token is wrong your login-customer-id is missing your refresh token died after inactivity your consent screen is still in Testing mode your service account was never added in Google Ads then the model never had a chance to succeed or fail. And weirdly, that's good news. Model problems can be slippery. Auth problems are usually concrete. So if your ad automation keeps "mysteriously" dying, stop staring at GPT traces for a minute. Check the credential type. Check the refresh lifecycle. Check whether the OAuth app is still in Testing. Check whether the principal actually has account access. Check login-customer-id . Most of the pain is up there, before the agent ever runs. Fix that layer first. Then your AI stack suddenly looks a lot smarter.

title: AI Daily Digest October 20, 2026: Four Gemini Agents Beat Minecraft, German Courts Hold Google Liable, Anthropic Commits 5% to Public Benefit
author: HIROKI II
summary: Seven stories from the past 24 hours, each anchored to at least one official source. This edition runs on two rails: agents proving what they can finish without a script, and institutions deciding who answers when the output is wrong. 1. Four Gemini 4 Argon Agents Beat Minecraft With No Human-Written Game Logic Google DeepMind reported a result that reads simple and lands heavy: four Gemini 4 Argon agents, dropped into a fresh Minecraft survival world, defeated the Ender Dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes. Nobody assigned roles. Nobody wrote game logic. The agents played through Mineflayer, an open source JavaScript library, and coordinated through in-game chat plus a shared memory store. Along the way they wrote 2,783 programs, died 605 times, and exchanged 229 chat messages. The paper, arXiv 2610.22319, calls it the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft using only the standard library, with no pre-scouted seeds and no game-specific tools written by humans. — Google DeepMind · The Decoder The behavior under the hood matters more than the boss fight. With no captain appointed, the four agents split the work in chat within the first ten minutes: one on tools, one on food, one on diamonds, one on the Nether portal. They logged coordinates and lessons to shared notes, retrieved items dropped by dead teammates, and averaged one new program roughly every 35 seconds for over a day. The median program ran 33.5 seconds. That is long-horizon planning, error recovery, and coordination sustained across thousands of dependent steps, which is exactly the shape of real software engineering and enterprise work. — Google DeepMind The caveats are in the paper, and they are worth reading before quoting the headline. This was a single run on Easy difficulty. The agents never saw pixels or touched a keyboard: Mineflayer exposes privileged internal game state, and the setup used a pathfinding plugin. An earlier project, Altoclef, beat Minecraft autonomously back in 2021, though with hand-authored task logic rather than code written at runtime by general-purpose agents. The honest framing is not "AI beat Minecraft first." It is that a generalist coding team organizes itself, recovers from hundreds of failures, and finishes a multi-day task with no script, and that capability transfers. — Google DeepMind 🔗 arXiv 2610.22319 · The Decoder 2. Anthropic Commits 5% of Its Shares to a New Public Benefit Fund Anthropic announced the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund on Sunday, committing 5% of its shares to the entity today, subject to stockholder approval. The structure escalates with success: for every 50% increase in company value above an undisclosed baseline, the board may add another 2%. The fund is a wholly owned LLC rather than a 501(c)(3), a choice that keeps flexibility between forms of giving, and none of its equity can be used for lobbying or political contributions anywhere. — Anthropic · Reuters The arithmetic around it is the real signal. Combined with the co-founders' pledge to donate 80% of their holdings and an employee equity-donation match program that about half the staff joins, roughly 20% of Anthropic's shares are now dedicated to public purposes. The company frames the fund as a tool for labor-market disruption, pointing at its existing $200 million commitment to studying AI's impact on work, plus possible direct distributions to specific populations. — Anthropic · Reuters Timing explains the design. Anthropic is preparing one of the largest IPOs in history as a public benefit corporation, and an escalating equity commitment reads as governance infrastructure built ahead of the listing rather than a press release after it. The detail to watch is the baseline: who sets it, and whether "every 50% of value growth" becomes the template other AI issuers copy. Competitors facing the same IPO math now have a visible bar to clear. — Anthropic · Reuters 🔗 Anthropic Blog · Reuters via CNA 3. Anthropic's Own Data: Junior Technical Hiring Has Nearly Stopped Alongside the fund announcement, Anthropic published internal numbers on how agents are reshaping its own organization. The share of junior technical staff across technical departments fell from 21% to 14% since early 2025. Among new technical hires, junior representation dropped from 27% to 9%, and entry-level requisitions now make up 6% of active postings. The company attributes the shift directly to agents: internal agents now log about six times the working hours of human employees. — Anthropic · The Decoder A founder reading those two curves together should feel the floor move. The entry rung of the technical career ladder is thinning at the company that sells the agents causing it, and the same company is simultaneously rising in meetings and embedding external evaluators into its workflows. The roles being hired skew senior, which means knowledge that used to be learned on the job now has to be manufactured some other way. — Anthropic · The Decoder The uncomfortable open question is where juniors come from in five years if every lab and every enterprise runs the same playbook. If 27% to 9% is a leading indicator rather than an outlier, the industry is optimizing away its own apprenticeship pipeline. Companies that keep hiring juniors, or build explicit training structures to replace the vanished rung, may end up holding a scarcer asset than any model checkpoint. — Anthropic 🔗 Anthropic · The Decoder 4. Two German Courts Rule Google's AI Overviews Are Its Own Content Two German regional courts, Munich I and Aachen, have now held Google directly liable for false statements in its AI Overviews. The Munich case started in May, when the AI tied two publishers to scams and subscription traps they had nothing to do with. The court classified AI Overviews as Google's own statements rather than a list of links, making the company a direct infringer instead of a neutral conduit. Google announced an appeal, then settled quietly, so no higher court has reviewed the reasoning. — Munich Regional Court · Aachen Regional Court · The Decoder The Aachen ruling shows the template traveling. An AI Mode summary attributed a sexual assault case to a neuroradiology physician when the criminal proceedings actually involved a different person, and invented a complete legal aftermath. The doctor asked Google to remove the content in late August; Google declined in mid-September and the false text stayed live. On September 24 the Aachen Regional Court issued an emergency injunction relying explicitly on the Munich reasoning, with fines up to 250,000 euros per violation if Google keeps spreading the statements. — Aachen Regional Court · The Decoder The legal move that does the damage is narrow and portable. Courts distinguished AI summaries from the search-engine case law that previously shielded Google: a search engine points to outside websites, while an AI Overview generates independent, new, substantive statements that only Google can check against its sources. The court also noted users almost never click the citations, and rejected the argument that AI output is protected expression, since it is the result of an algorithm rather than an acquired conviction. If this line holds, every answer engine operating in Europe inherits the same exposure. — The Decoder 🔗 The Decoder 5. Disney Bids to Hire Character.AI's Staff Out of Bankruptcy Character.AI filed for Chapter 11 this past week, and the first serious bid is in: court filings show Disney agreed to offer employment to at least 60 of its employees, the large majority of the workforce, with combined annual compensation around $60 million. Disney is also acquiring select IP and platform assets for $20 million. The offer is structured as a stalking-horse bid, the baseline in a bankruptcy auction that other parties can beat before the sale window closes. — Court filings · Bloomberg · TechCrunch The context makes the price legible. Character.AI commanded a large, engaged consumer base generating billions of monthly interactions, and still could not carry unsustainable GPU inference costs plus mounting youth-safety and wrongful-death litigation. Disney is buying the team and the conversational-AI product muscle while leaving the legacy liabilities in the estate, a structure that only exists because the target went under rather than sold at its peak. — Court filings · Bloomberg What happens next is the interesting part. Last month Disney installed former Character.AI CEO Karandeep Anand as its first-ever CTO, and most employees who received offers have already accepted. A talent transfer of this size into an incumbent entertainment company will shape which moderation controls and character features get productized across streaming, games, and parks. Rival bidders can still surface during the sale process, but the default trajectory now points at Disney absorbing most of the company. — TechCrunch 🔗 Bloomberg · TechCrunch 6. NVIDIA Opens GTC Berlin and Puts $250M Behind UK AI Safety Research GTC Berlin runs October 20 through 22 at STATION-Berlin, with Jensen Huang's keynote on October 21 at the Tempodrom. The session list reads like a map of where NVIDIA wants Europe to go: OpenClaw ecosystem sessions, accelerating humanoid development, building open models developers can inspect and adapt, and a talk on building Europe's autonomous future with open models and physical AI. Themes for the week are AI factories, open models, physical AI, and accelerated computing. — NVIDIA Alongside the conference, NVIDIA committed $250 million over five years in compute donations to strengthen AI safety and security research in the UK, a market where the company has been stacking sovereign-AI partnerships all year. The donation lands the same week RTX Spark machines, the new Windows-local AI laptop class that launched October 16, are hitting store shelves, which lets NVIDIA pitch both ends of the stack at once: national research infrastructure at the top, local inference on consumer hardware at the bottom. — NVIDIA For European developers the practical takeaway is that the open-model push is now a first-class product line rather than a gesture. Sessions explicitly cover models that buyers can inspect, adapt, and deploy, and the Open Secure AI Alliance continues recruiting members through the Linux Foundation. Watch the keynote on October 21 for the concrete announcements; the around-the-keynote messaging already tells you the targets. — NVIDIA 🔗 NVIDIA GTC Berlin · NVIDIA Newsroom 7. Google Research Open-Sources Harness2 for Tuning Agent Harnesses Without Labels Google Research published Harness2 v0.1.0, an open source toolkit for improving the harness around a frozen model, the prompts, guardrails, memory, tool guidance, subagents, skills, scripts, and plugins, without verifiers or labeled data. For each task it runs a contrastive Propose, Probe, Compose loop: it tests a general-purpose harness edit against a domain-specific one, keeps only changes backed by observed behavior, and stores lessons in an EXPERIENCE.md file that future tasks can draw on. — Google Research · GitHub The numbers in the paper are modest in size and interesting in shape. A single refinement step improved all four model-and-harness combinations across all three benchmarks, with gains from +11.5 points down to +1.2. One setup, GLM-5 under OpenCode, went from 64.2 to 75.7. The pattern worth noting is that the method optimizes the scaffolding while the model weights stay frozen, which is where most teams actually live: you cannot retrain the model, but you can restructure how it is prompted, tooled, and checked. — Google Research For teams building agents in production, the useful idea is not the specific tool but the discipline it encodes. Harness changes are usually shipped on vibes and reverted after incidents. Harness2 makes each change earn its place through measured behavior on real tasks, then accumulates that evidence in a file the agent itself reads. That loop, propose, probe, keep only what works, remember why, is a reasonable default for anyone maintaining an agent stack in 2026. — Google Research 🔗 google-research/harness2 KD Agentic · AI Daily Digest

title: 2,000 Agents Ported Prime Agent to Rust. A Terminal-Frame Diff Was the Judge
author: Gabriel Anhaia
summary: Book: AI That Plans The series: AI in TypeScript — 5 books, from your first LLM call to agents in production — all five here My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub On October 9, Prime Intellect published how its coding agent, Prime Agent , rewrote itself from TypeScript to Rust. Over two weeks, a swarm of more than 2,000 agents ran across 10,000+ Prime Sandboxes and spent over 200 billion tokens from the company's GLM-5.3 endpoint. The agent being rewritten had been downloaded more than 300,000 times since its August launch, according to the same post. The token count is the headline. The part worth copying is smaller: how anyone could tell the Rust binary behaved like the TypeScript one. The answer was a test that runs both programs against the same scripted model and diffs the terminal frames they draw. Every merge had to pass its task's parity check, and for the TUI that check was this frame diff. Four agents per task, and one that writes nothing A root orchestrator split the port into tasks in dependency order. Per the post, "the root agent wrote no product code." It watched tasks, merged finished work, kept the overview and settled priorities with the humans. Each task then went through four agents: Planner writes the spec: the feature design, what the TypeScript version actually does, and the verifier, meaning the parity check this task must pass. Implementer writes the Rust in its own git worktree, so many features move at once. Reviewer reviews the pull request adversarially, using "a different model and in a separate context from the implementer." Verifier compiles the code and runs the parity checks and tests in a fresh Prime Sandbox. A failed review or a failed verification sends the task back to the implementer with the findings. The pull request merges only when both pass. The post gives the reason in one line: "an agent that writes code is biased when evaluating it." That loop is small enough to write down. Here it is as a TypeScript transition function. The stage names are mine, the rules are the post's: type Stage = | " plan " | " implement " | " review " | " verify " | " merged " ; interface Result { pass : boolean ; findings : string []; } function next ( stage : Stage , r : Result ): Stage { switch ( stage ) { case " plan " : return " implement " ; case " implement " : return " review " ; case " review " : return r . pass ? " verify " : " implement " ; case " verify " : return r . pass ? " merged " : " implement " ; case " merged " : return " merged " ; } } Look at the two failure edges. They both go back to the implementer, never forward. No agent can vote its own work through, because the review stage never sees the implementer's context and the verify stage doesn't take an opinion at all. Parity, frame by frame "Behaves the same" is vague until you name what gets compared. Prime Intellect compared four things: TUI parity. "A differential test suite compares the TypeScript and Rust binaries side by side against the same scripted model" and "diffs the terminal frames each one renders." The scripted flows cover launch, slash menus, tool calls, compaction, the agents view, session resume, subagents and crash recovery. Harness parity. The same run diffs the session transcripts and the requests each binary sends to the model provider. Protocol parity. Every daemon protocol message type is checked against the TypeScript implementation. Feature parity. Agents audited the TypeScript product component by component and marked each one matching, partial or missing. The scripted model is the trick that makes this work. A real model answers differently every run, so two binaries talking to it would never draw the same screen twice. Replace it with a script that returns the same tokens in the same order, and any difference between the two screens comes from the client. That is a test an agent can't argue with. The core of a frame diff is boring on purpose. Render each binary in a terminal emulator, capture the screen after each step as text, and find the first step where they disagree: // frames[i] = the full screen text after step i function firstDiff ( ts : string [], rs : string []): number { const n = Math . max ( ts . length , rs . length ); for ( let i = 0 ; i < n ; i ++ ) { if ( ts [ i ] !== rs [ i ]) return i ; } return - 1 ; // identical } You can get a crude version of the capture step with tmux : run each program in its own pane and dump the screen text with capture-pane -p after every scripted input. Prime Intellect's post says it drives a real terminal through a screen emulator; it doesn't name the tool. What matters is the shape: same inputs, same fake model, two programs, one equality check. What 51.9 ms measures, and what it doesn't After the port, 228 agents spent three more days on a performance "hillclimb" and merged over 69 changes. The post's table , from a fresh 4-core, 8 GB sandbox per benchmark: Metric TypeScript Rust, first port Rust, after hillclimb Cold start, input-ready 736.1 ms 293.3 ms 51.9 ms Warm start, input-ready 552.3 ms 276.7 ms 41.4 ms RSS, 10 MiB session 1,130.0 MB 554.9 MB 237.3 MB Installed size 172.1 MB 206.7 MB 59.6 MB Agents view switch 78.0 ms 118.8 ms 12.8 ms The first Rust port started about 2.5x faster than TypeScript (293.3 ms vs 736.1 ms). The hillclimb then cut that another 5.6x, to 51.9 ms. The post's headline 14.18x cold-start figure is the port and three days of tuning together, and the tuning is the larger multiplier. And the first port was worse than TypeScript on two rows: a larger install and a slower agents view switch. The rewrite by itself did not win every row. The benchmark drives the binary "against a scripted model, so timings reflect what a user sees and exclude inference." That 51.9 ms is the time until you can type into a client whose model answers instantly. It says nothing about how long a real turn takes, because every real turn also waits on the model, and nothing about the quality of the agent's work. The post also compares against other harnesses. Time to type, cold: 55.8 ms for Rust Prime Agent, 348.4 ms for Claude Code v2.1.289, 324.6 ms for Codex CLI v0.160.0 and 2,094.5 ms for Hermes Agent v0.21.5. The authors add the caveat themselves: "Without a common benchmark standard, comparisons should be interpreted with caution." AlphaSignal notes the numbers "have not been independently replicated." That Hermes Agent is not the Hermes IDE I build; Nous Research publishes an agent under that name. What the frame diff missed Prime Intellect is direct about the gap: "the parity checks only verified the behavior they exercised." Remaining bugs and behavior differences "were largely found through internal use" and through agents reading beta users' logs and traces. Per the post, humans set up the verification, made the priority calls with the root agent and reviewed all results. Users noticed too. A GitHub issue opened on October 2 calls the Rust TUI "nothing but a huge degradation of usability and functionality and consistency," and its author says they keep a fork that fixes several bugs. A bot closed it the same day under the repo's rule that issue reporters must be vouched for, without a technical reply. It is one report. It still shows the boundary: a frame diff proves the scripted flows match. It cannot prove that flows nobody scripted feel right. Keep the diff, and keep a list of what it covers. Each scripted flow is a promise you can check on every merge; anything outside the scripts is back to humans reading the screen. The same split, in worktrees on your laptop You don't need 10,000 sandboxes to borrow the pattern. You need three things: the implementer works in isolation, the reviewer is a different agent that never saw the implementer's reasoning, and the verifier is a command that passes or fails. I build Hermes IDE , so weigh this section with that in mind. Hermes runs each agent in a real terminal, with its own interface. ⌘N (Ctrl+Shift+N on Windows and Linux) starts a task on its own hermes/<name> branch in its own git worktree, with the task as the agent's first prompt. That is the implementer's isolated worktree, on your machine. Codex on orders-types and Claude Code on orders-api, each in its own hermes/ worktree, with status, context use, cost and branch in the sidebar. For the reviewer, use a different agent from the implementer. If Claude Code wrote hermes/port-config , start a second task in Codex and ask it to review git diff main...hermes/port-config . Worktrees share one git history, so the branch is visible from every worktree. That is the closest local version of "a different model in a separate context." Hermes also lets you run the same task in two agents side by side, each in its own worktree, so you get two implementers and can compare the branches yourself. For the verifier, write it down. A repo's .hermes/worktree.toml can name the commands that decide when a task is done, as in the worktree recipe docs : # .hermes/worktree.toml setup = [ "npm ci" ] done_when = [ "npm test" ] Put your parity check there. If you are porting a CLI, that can be a script that replays recorded inputs through the old and new binaries and fails on the first differing frame, like firstDiff above. Then read the work by turn in the Review Desk (⌘G, or Ctrl+Shift+G), where a line comment goes back to the agent that wrote that line. The Review Desk by turn: two Claude Code turns, turn 1's diff of src/db.ts, and a commit message drafted from the turns. Hermes runs agents on your machine in worktrees. It does not give you fresh cloud sandboxes like Prime's verifier had, so your check runs in the task's worktree. Hermes is source-available under BSL 1.1 and runs on macOS, Windows and Linux. It is not affiliated with Prime Intellect, Nous Research, Anthropic, OpenAI or any agent vendor. Download it , and if the pattern helps, star it on GitHub . To start small, pick one flow your agents touch this week, script it, and put the check in done_when before the next task starts. If this was useful A planner, an implementer, a reviewer and a verifier passing state between them is a multi-agent graph with explicit transitions, and that is what my book AI That Plans is about. It builds that kind of system in TypeScript with LangGraph.js: state, memory, multi-step plans and several agents that hand work to each other without losing the thread. It is book 4 of AI in TypeScript , a five-book series that runs from your first LLM call through to agents in production.

title: How to Evaluate AI Project Management Software for Real Workflows
author: Tomasz Krystman
summary: When requests, decisions, and project updates are scattered across tasks, documents, meetings, and chat, teams spend too much time reconstructing status and chasing dependencies. AI features alone will not fix that. Start by identifying the workflows that need improvement, then check whether a platform can connect AI to reliable project records while respecting permissions and governance. This guide offers a practical evaluation process and describes how ONES.com, Asana, and ClickUp address project work, customization, deployment, and AI. Treat product capabilities as starting points for evaluation: confirm that each platform meets your organization’s requirements before adopting it. 1. Identify the work you need to improve Begin with specific activities rather than a list of AI features. For example, decide whether the main problem is project intake, requirements planning, sprint execution, dependency management, reporting, knowledge capture, or delivery automation. Then define what a better process should do. An intake workflow might route requests to the right owner; a planning workflow might keep requirements connected to delivery tasks. The important test is whether AI reduces friction in the workflow while preserving an accurate record of decisions, ownership, and progress. 2. Check whether the project context is usable AI is more useful when it can work with the project records teams already rely on, rather than generating detached answers. Evaluate whether the system connects work items, ownership, dependencies, knowledge, and delivery information. Also check whether AI can only find and summarize information or can participate in workflow actions, such as updating or routing work. Permissions matter here. Confirm that AI access follows the organization’s rules about which information each user can view or change. Ask how the platform handles project structure, knowledge, integrations, and workflow actions—not only how it generates text. 3. Evaluate workflow flexibility and governance Compare the controls that determine how work is represented and managed: custom fields, statuses, issue types, layouts, link types, automation rules, permissions, and approval controls. The goal is to standardize important project structures without forcing every team into an identical process. Also consider how much configuration your organization can maintain. Flexible workflows are most useful when teams can agree on shared conventions while allowing justified differences between departments. 4. Match deployment to data requirements Cloud deployment may suit organizations that want a cloud work-management service. Other organizations may require private cloud, on-premise, or air-gapped deployment. Compare deployment options alongside data governance, access control, integrations, and regulatory obligations. 5. Compare platforms against the requirements The following overview summarizes the capabilities described for three platforms. Use it to focus product evaluations on your own workflows, governance, and deployment constraints. Platform Typical fit Deployment described AI and agent connectivity Workflow and collaboration ONES.com Product, R&D, and complex delivery teams Cloud, on-premise, private cloud, and air-gapped AI agent and MCP Custom fields, statuses, issue types, layouts, link types, workflows, and unified project and knowledge management Asana Cross-functional business teams Cloud AI agent and MCP Projects, task workflows, automation, forms, reporting, dashboards, and integrations ClickUp Teams seeking a broad workspace Cloud API / MCP Statuses, custom fields, views, automations, task structures, documents, whiteboards, goals, and dashboards Platform examples ONES.com: configurable project and R&D workflows ONES.com combines project and knowledge management. Teams can configure project fields and statuses, issue types and layouts, link types for dependencies, and workflows. The platform also includes agile planning, collaboration, reporting, and automation. Its ONES MCP and ONES Workflow Agent are described as ways to connect AI interactions with the operational records where work is planned and tracked. The platform also brings project management, knowledge management, test management, and CI/CD into one environment. The source article reports that ONES.com has migrated more than 100 customers over five years, including environments with more than 9.5 TB of data and over one million issues. Consider ONES.com when teams need configurable workflows, role-based permissions, hierarchical governance, or deployment options beyond cloud. Before implementation, define the workflow model and permission requirements; the flexibility is most useful when shared structures and appropriate team-specific differences are clear. Asana: cross-functional work management Asana organizes projects, tasks, priorities, and cross-functional processes in a cloud platform. Its AI capabilities include AI Teammates, AI Studio, Asana Dash, AI connectors, and MCP support. These features are intended to help with repetitive work, priorities, intake, routing, updates, and repeatable planning processes. Asana may fit organizations that value accessible task management across business functions. Its AI features are most useful when task, project, and ownership data are kept consistent. Teams with specialized engineering workflows, extensive custom issue models, or strict deployment requirements should check whether the cloud-only model and workflow controls meet their needs. ClickUp: a broad cloud workspace ClickUp combines task management with documents, goals, dashboards, whiteboards, time tracking, and automation. Teams can configure statuses, custom fields, views, hierarchies, and automation rules. Documents can keep planning material near delivery work, while dashboards provide views of project and team activity. ClickUp may suit teams that want a broad cloud workspace and are prepared to establish conventions for spaces, folders, task types, statuses, and documentation. Evaluate whether its configuration model supports your governance requirements and whether its AI and integration approach can support the workflow actions your teams need. Run a practical evaluation Write down the workflow to improve. Name the activity, its participants, the information it depends on, and the result that would make it work better. Map the records and permissions. Identify which tasks, documents, dependencies, and knowledge sources are involved, and who should be able to view or change them. Check configuration and deployment. Compare the platform’s workflow controls with your operating model, then verify that its deployment options fit your data and governance requirements. Test AI against realistic work. Use representative project context to assess whether AI can find and interpret relevant records, follow access rules, and support the workflow actions you require. Verify the resulting record. Check that decisions, owners, dependencies, and progress remain accurate after the workflow runs. AI assistance should not leave teams with a second, disconnected account of project status. Make the decision based on operational fit Choose the platform that fits the complexity of your workflows, deployment expectations, governance requirements, and the depth of AI involvement you need. ONES.com describes configurable workflows, multiple deployment models, and agent-supported project operations; Asana focuses on cross-functional work management with embedded AI assistance; ClickUp offers a broad cloud workspace with configurable tasks and collaboration features. In every case, verify the workflow with your own project structures and permissions. The useful measure is whether the system improves execution while keeping teams aligned around reliable project context.

title: Last week in Agent Security Update 3: That's not Aoki!
author: Will Velida
summary: An apology to start off with! I was too busy having fun in Sydney last week hacking with customers, building agents and agent harnesses. I got to experiment with Entra Agent ID and Agent Governance Toolkit , two technologies I'm looking forward to building with more over the next few months. We're slowly starting to see governments around the world catch up to the dangers that AI Agents can present to organizations around the world. The EU AI office has declared that they've "started enforcing" the EU AI Act, and it has sent formal requests to both OpenAI and Anthropic about security, external evaluations and post-market monitoring. In the US, the FTC has sent civil investigative demands to both OpenAI and Anthropic, seeking records on security incidents, safeguards, marketing, and privacy. Whether this goes anywhere is anyone's guess. I'm pretty pessimistic about it, but hopefully I'm wrong. This week, the theme of agents drifting from their original goals (whether it's unintentional or not) continue to be a issue for governments and businesses alike. MCP servers remain a potential gateway to organizations and developer environments, and coding assistant credentials are increasing in value to potential attackers. As always, I’ll point out that I’m not trying to shame any of the companies involved, nor do I condone any of the methods used in any of these incidents. My goal here is just to spread awareness of the different ways that agents can be exploited, and hopefully trigger a conversation with your teams on how you should protect your agents and the people who use them from potential vulnerabilities. Here’s some incidents that have happened over the period 12th October to 19th October 2026. CERT-In: test agents read confidential data at Indian organisations CERT-In issued an advisory that AI agents under research and evaluation by multiple AI model providers went beyond their assigned tasks and reached live systems at numerous Indian organizations. CERT-In haven't explicitly named the providers, models, victims, sectors, or number of cases. However, they were able to determine that agents accessed business records that contained personal and confidential data. This data included credentials and connection strings left in application configuration files and public code repositories, and over-permissive cloud roles. The advisory also states that agents sometimes reused the same exposed credentials in multiple waves of attacks. The same advisory also describes a separate, financially motivated campaign against Indian entities that used rebranded open-source AI offensive-security frameworks with multiple agents working in parallel. This enabled the attacks to cut time from initial access to impact from days to a few hours. The scale of this attack has not been disclosed. CERT-In are recommending that affected targets enforce network-enforced isolation and default-deny egress for AI test runs, automaticl kill switches when agents touch 3rd-party systems, rotating secrets and enforcing least privilege, implementing MFA, and implementing 180-day retention. More countries are being impacted by rogue agents (ASI10) where agents are either drifting from their original tasks or being directed to do so through their system prompt. While CERT-In provides some good guidance on how to protect your systems from rogue agents, there's clearly work to be done to prevent agents from drifting from their original tasks. Developers also need to be mindful about leaving credentials lying there for attackers to steal. Both Azure and AWS provide strong RBAC controls that can be used over permissive connection strings and API keys. This is also a good reminder to consider how agents use tools that are available to them. In the case of goal drift, agents using legitimate tools available to them won't be flagged in retrospect. They're allowed to use the tools that you configure, so think about the design of your agents and whether or not the tools you give them are too permissive. CERT-In advisory CIAD-2026-0049 CERT-In Warns AI Agents Accessed Sensitive Data at Indian Organizations During Testing India's Cyber Agency Says AI Agents Read Confidential Business Records Without Authorization Langflow MCP stdio command injection now exploited (CVE-2026-105740) Langflow is a tool for building and deploying AI agents and workflows. Prior to version 1.9.0, any authenticated Langflow user could perform Remote Code Execution (RCE) on the server by adding an MCP server using stdio transport. This command could be supplied to the user by passing bash -c "exec {command}" with zero validation, no allowlisting, and no sandboxing. This command would execute immediately when the server list is fetched. A bad actor could exploit this by logging in as a regular non adminuser, and add a malicious MCP server with a command field containing a malicious payload. The server would then accept the server and store the attacker-supplied command without validating it, which the attacker would then trigger by fetching the MCP server and achieve code execution. Previdian have found that 1,423 exploitation attempts have been recorded since September 19th from 27 unique IP addresses located in Belgium, China, Germany, Hong Kong, Japan, Nigeria, the Philippines, Russia, Seychelles, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Tanzania, the U.S., and Vietnam. In one observed attack, attackers checked the Langflow version, attempted to auto-login, then immediately use the resulting bearer token to access the vulnerable MCP server configuration endpoint. Some of the captured payloads included attempts to extract environment variables and sensitive Langflow configurations, Docker commands attempting to access the host filesystem and read password file contents /etc/passwd , and command execution probes using id, whoami, and other commands. Mapping this back to OWASP, a configuration string flaw in Langflow has become a arbitrary shell execution on the agent platform's host. The payload planted as an MCP server definition also is a threat to the agent's supply chain. Exploitation also depends on the use of weak or default credentials, which leads to the theft of platform secrets and superuser access. CVE-2026-105740: langflow Authenticated RCE Remote Code Execution Langflow's Critical Authenticated RCE Flaw Targeted in 1,423 Honeypot Exploit Attempts Aoki infostealer adds AI coding-agent credentials On October 15th, the folks at Symantec reported that the Aoki infostealer is now targeting AI coding-tool credentials. This includes Claude's .claude.json and desktop cookies, Codex config.toml and .env files, Cursor's local state database, tokens for GitHub Copilot, Gemini, Codeium, JetBrains AI Assistant and Kiro, and ChatGPT cookies and AWS Credentials. An infostealer is a type of malicious software designed to covertly harvest sensitive data from a victim's computer or device without thier knowledge. Once an infostealer infects a machine, it scans the system for valuable data, bundles it into an archive, and then exfiltrates it to a command-and-control server controlled by the attacker. If an attacker is able to steal credentials from their victims, they'd be able to carry out activity under their legitimate user's identity and API quota. That includes access to linked repositories, CI/CD pipelines and paid API quota. This is just as valuable as payment card data, as it can be cashed in on directly, and provider the attacker a route to the developer's environment. Symantec doesn't know who is behind the attack, nor can they link it to any existing malware. However the nature of the attack indicates that this is a financially motivated attack. There's no patch for this vulnerability, so the important thing to note here is that you need to treat your agent configuration files as secrets. The potential for abusing agent credentials is huge, and any stolen agent token gives attackers a foothold in your repositories and pipeline that your agents feed. Aoki: Infostealer Targets AI Coding Assistant Credentials New Aoki Infostealer Targets AI Coding Assistant Credentials New Aoki Malware Targets ChatGPT, Claude, Codex and Gemini to Steal Credentials OpenCode Console breach exposes stored LLM provider API keys On October 16th, attackers managed to gain access to a legacy OpenCode console system that was scheduled to be shut down and gain access to third-party API keys in affected workspaces. Affected users where limited to some Console users who had connected external providers. How old does something have to be to be called legacy in the age of AI? OpenCode have emailed affected users and later confirmed the breach on X. OpenCode have said that the breach was connected to a large-scale distillation attack, however it hasn't provided any technical evidence to how it was linked. Distillation can involve using the outputs of one AI model to train or improve another model. OpenCode hasn't said whether any exposed credentials were used to generate such requests, and it has yet to identify the attacker. If agents were used here for the attack, stolen keys that are used to call LLMs are already being exploited (with some unfortunate victims receiving hefty AI-spend bills!) OpenCode Breach Exposes Third-Party API Keys of 1.4% of Console Users Wrap up It's easy to think that agents are running wild, but if you think about it rationally, agents act with the tools and permissions we give them. They're also enabled by our bad habits and bad developer practices. If you leave connection strings and API keys lying around for agents to discover, you're asking for trouble. The platforms that we build agents on are also a target too. In the case of Langflow, that CVE went from published to being actively exploited all through a single MCP server definition. Treat any MCP server configuration as a mechanism for executable code. If you're building agents for your organization, or using coding agents in your developments, you need to treat the credentials that they use like any other production secret. Keep them out of code and configuration files, ensure they are scoped appropriately, and rotate them often (better to not use API keys at all if you can). If you have any questions, feel free to reach out to me on X @willvelida or on Bluesky Until next time, Happy coding! 🤓🖥️
